From maritime security to trusted supply chains, new technologies and disaster response, our endeavour is to ensure that the Quad delivers trusted solutions to the entire Indo-Pacific,” Modi said in his opening remarks at the meeting. Modi announced Mumbai will host the inaugural Quad Business Leaders Forum in early 2027, while Trump said the grouping will conduct its first military exercise with maritime patrol aircraft to “protect peace through strength”. “As four major market economies, we have a shared responsibility to create greater trade opportunities and build stronger supply chains. To turn our strategic cooperation into commercial partnerships, India has announced the Quad Business Leaders Forum,” Modi said. The forum will gather business leaders, government officials and policy experts to foster greater business ties across private sectors, including the promotion of commercial deals and partnerships, a joint press release said. “If Australia's mining experience, Japan's recycling technology, America's expertise and India's manufacturing base come together, they could provide new strength to supply chains,” Modi added. The Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, which takes forward the Quad’s earlier maritime domain awareness initiative, is meant to enhance information-sharing and maritime awareness. The P-8 and P-3 maritime patrol aircraft of the four countries will join “a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making our seas safer”, the release said. This exercise will be conducted on the sidelines of Exercise Sea Dragon in Guam in March 2027 to address shared challenges such as illegal fishing and trafficking, foreign secretary Vikram Misri said. The four leaders also announced an expansion of the Quad Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience, currently focused on the safety of telecommunications cables. “This will now expand to undersea energy cables as well,” Misri said, referring to Australia’s contribution focused on electricity cables to strengthen regional energy security. The four countries also welcomed upcoming undersea cable projects in the Indian Ocean intended to strengthen regional connectivity. The Quad acknowledged a “rapid increase in the number and scale of cyber incidents” in the region and announced enhanced cybersecurity cooperation between the four countries to “achieve an open and secure cyberspace”. This was an apparent reference to China's assertive actions in the South China Sea, where it is engaged in territorial disputes with several Asean states. The Quad expressed “grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions” – again, an apparent reference to China's restrictions on the export of crucial commodities such as rare earths and fertilisers. The Quad nations said they are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through future technologies, including investments in trusted Artificial Intelligence (AI), and responding to disasters with life-saving assistance. “We commit to work together to ensure open, safe, and resilient maritime transit corridors in the Indo-Pacific,” the press release added. Modi noted that the Quad's maritime domain awareness partnership has already created a real-time data sharing mechanism that is used to address illegal fishing and illicit activities in the Indo-Pacific, and said the grouping should aim to promote peace and prosperity, economic and technological resilience, and delivery of public goods. “Safeguarding maritime security begins with ensuring the safety of the seafarers who keep it moving,” Modi said. “Therefore, we must work together to establish a robust international framework for the safety of seafarers. This was the seventh Quad Summit and the first to be held outside the member countries. However, Manila has a special connection with Quad – it was in the Philippines capital that officials of the grouping first met in 2007, and activities of the grouping were subsequently revived after a hiatus at a meeting held in the city in 2017. The four countries also unequivocally condemned all forms of terrorism and violent extremism, including cross-border terrorism, and said they are committed to strengthening Quad’s ongoing cooperation on counter-terrorism. There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority. According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman. There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost. They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control. All settlements are illegal under international law. - UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements Published 2 hours ago Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home. Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said. According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat. "My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said. "My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot." She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting." Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?" Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle". Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat." Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses. The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement. Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents. A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month. A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo) In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent. The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident. Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now. It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank". The UK government announced on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank. It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
